1:
Who incited David is the first and hardest question, and the witnesses divide on grammar. Ellicott would render it that an adversary arose against Israel, and argues from the article: when the enemy of mankind is meant the Hebrew word takes it, and here it does not. Since the parallel says instead that the anger of the Lord burned and that he incited David, Ellicott concludes the adversary here is the wrath of God, which he defines as that aspect of the divine nature which pursues to destruction whatever is opposed to its own perfection. On his reading the wrath could only have urged David in consequence of evil thoughts of pride intruding into a heart until then humbly reliant on its Maker: one evil thought led to another by the laws God has imposed on human nature, and God did not interpose but let a corrupt motive work out its own penal results. He adds that the true reading in Samuel may be that an adversary incited David, the word having dropped out.

Henry and Wesley keep the person and distribute the blame. Henry grants that numbering a people is in itself no bad thing, since a shepherd may know the number of his flock, and locates the fault wholly in the pride of David's heart, no sin having more of contradiction in it, and so more offence to God, than pride. The sin was David's, he insists, and he alone must bear the blame; yet Satan is active in it, aiming as always to weaken the strength and eclipse the glory of God's Israel. Where Samuel says God moved David, Henry explains that God is not the author of sin and tempts no man, so the moving must mean that for wise and holy ends he permitted the devil to do it; and warns that even the best saints, until they come to heaven, must never think themselves out of reach of Satan's temptations. Wesley stages it legally: Satan stood before the Lord's tribunal to accuse David and Israel and beg permission to tempt him, standing being the accuser's posture before human tribunals, which is why scripture speaks of the things of God after the manner of men.

The order given Joab is read as military, and closely compared. Ellicott infers the military character from the agents, Joab and the captains of the people being deputed to take it, and notes that the older book names only Joab while associating the captains with him elsewhere; he marks the verb as enrol or register, a different word from the one used two verses earlier, and observes that Samuel's run over all the tribes uses the very word Satan uses in Job for his own wanderings over the earth. The direction is unusual too, from Beersheba to Dan where the reverse is common. Delitzsch agrees that Joab was assisted by the captains of the host, and observes that the two accounts agree in the main points and use the same terms in many places, which shows both were drawn from one source.

Joab's protest is then weighed clause by clause. Ellicott renders the wish literally, that Jehovah add upon his people a hundred times as many, and calls it an abridgement of Samuel; where this text asks why the king should become a cause of trespass to Israel, Samuel has nothing, so the clause is the chronicler's explanatory addition. Delitzsch defends the shorter form against the doubled phrase in Samuel, taking the repetition there for a peculiarity of that writer and this expression for one that matches Deuteronomy. Wesley reads the trespass clause as a question about punishment and answers it with a rule: God commonly punishes a people for the sins of their rulers, because they are for the most part guilty of the same sins in one kind or another.
4:
Joab goes out, and Ellicott supplies from the older book what this one leaves out: the route across Jordan to Aroer and Jazer and Gilead and Dan, then round to Zidon and the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivite and the Canaanite, coming out at last in the south of Judah at Beersheba. The business occupied nine months and twenty days, and he draws a date from that figure. The commander of David's forces and his chief officers could only have found leisure for such an undertaking in a time of settled peace, so the census belongs to the later years of the reign.

The totals do not agree with the parallel, and Ellicott offers three ways out. Clarke simply sets the figures side by side, since the older book has eight hundred thousand for Israel and five hundred thousand for Judah where this one has eleven hundred thousand and four hundred and seventy thousand. Ellicott takes Judah's five hundred thousand for a round number and this text's figure as the more exact, and for the larger discrepancy allows either an error of transcription or, more probably, that the traditions about the census varied, which could easily happen since the numbers were never registered in the royal archives. His own preference is arithmetical: if the estimate here includes David's standing army, reckoned elsewhere at some three hundred thousand men, then the eight hundred thousand of the older account and that army together make the eleven hundred thousand of this one.

Why two tribes were left uncounted draws three different answers. Ellicott finds the exemption natural, a sacerdotal tribe having no place in a census taken for military or political purposes, and reminds the reader that the work was expressly never completed; the order in which the tribes were taken makes it likely that Judah and Benjamin were to come last, so that Joab, having numbered Judah, returned to the capital and was ordered to desist. Josephus, he adds, speaks as though Joab had simply not had time for Benjamin, and may have feared to give offence to the tribe of Saul. Clarke reports the rabbinic explanation, which makes it deliberate: Joab, foreseeing that the census would bring destruction on the people, purposed to save two tribes, and had an answer ready for each question the king might ask, that the Levites were not reckoned among the children of Israel, and that Benjamin had been punished enough already for the business of the woman at Gibeah, so that another punishment would leave none of them. Wesley makes it providence rather than policy, Levi being devoted to God's service and Benjamin the least of the tribes and once almost extinguished, and God foreseeing that they would be faithful to the house of David when the tribes divided, so that he would not have them diminished; though Wesley allows Joab his specious pretences too, that Levi were no warriors and the command reached only those who drew sword, and that Benjamin, being small and bordering on Jerusalem, could easily be numbered later.
7:
The chapter's verdict arrives before its narrative does. Ellicott notes that the sentence has no counterpart in Samuel, which reads instead that David's heart smote him after he had numbered the people, and that the peculiarities of expression there suggest textual corruption; the chronicler's line works as a general heading, an anticipative summary of everything that follows. Wesley supplies the ground of the displeasure: the thing was done without any colour of necessity, out of mere curiosity and ostentation. Henry takes the measure of it from the other side, as a man under the rod for the foolishness of pride. No sin, he says, is more displeasing to God than pride of heart, and nothing is more humbling and mortifying to a gracious soul than to see itself under that displeasure.

Confession follows at once, and Ellicott traces the chronicler's hand through it. The verse is word for word the parallel save for the characteristic substitution of God for Jehovah, the explanatory addition of this thing, and the dropping of the divine name from the second half; do away is literally cause to pass over. David's conscience misgave him in the night, before the interview with the prophet. At the next verse Samuel's wording — a word of Jehovah had come to Gad the prophet, a seer of David — looks the more original, and the title is better rendered a seer of David's, since the same phrase is used of Heman. From the later notice of Gad's writings it has been inferred that Gad composed the original record of the census.

The three penalties are then laid out, and Ellicott illustrates them from outside the Bible, quoting a curse from the Annals of Tiglath Pileser I which calls down on an enemy the overthrow of his army, pestilence to cut off his land, and want of crops and famine. On the terms themselves he prefers the chronicler: three years' famine harmonises with the three months and the three days, while Samuel's seven perhaps originated in a scribe's memory of the famine of Genesis. Clarke registers the same divergence from Samuel without adjudicating it. Whether this fuller text expands Samuel or Samuel epitomises it, Ellicott leaves open, noting the argument that the angel is otherwise introduced quite abruptly, and that in the thought of those times pestilence and the sword of the Lord were suggestive of each other.

What the choice cost the chooser is where the voices converge. Henry sees a man put into a strait for his further humiliation, with the terror of all three judgments impressed on his mind while he considers which to take. Clarke preserves the Targum's reconstruction of the reasoning: if David chose famine, Israel might say the granaries of David are full of corn and he cares nothing though the people die of hunger; if he chose flight before an enemy, they might say he is a strong and warlike man who cares nothing though they fall by the sword; so he delivers himself into the hand of the Word of the Lord, whose mercies are many, and not into the hands of the children of men. Ellicott reads the same decision as a confession of inability to choose, clear only that it is better to depend on the compassion of God than of man, which rules out the second alternative and leaves the rest to God. Henry's gloss is briefer: good men, even when God frowns upon them, think well of him.
14:
The toll is reported and then immediately abridged. Ellicott observes that the opening clause follows Samuel and that the rest of the verse is cut short, so that it is from Samuel we learn how long the plague raged: throughout the land, from dawn to the hour of the evening sacrifice. Wesley reads the arithmetic as judgment answering the sin that provoked it — David was proud of the number of his people, and God took a course to make them fewer, for justly is that which we are proud of taken from us or embittered to us.

At the stay of the plague Clarke turns aside to the Targum, which supplies a whole scene the Hebrew does not. There the Word of the Lord sends the angel of death against Jerusalem, and the angel, looking down, beholds the ashes of the binding of Isaac at the foot of the altar; and God remembers the covenant with Abraham made in the Mount of Worship, and the house of the upper sanctuary where the souls of the righteous are, and the image of Jacob fixed upon the throne of glory, and turns from the evil he had designed, saying to the destroying angel, Cease. Ellicott works the same verse as a textual problem instead. Samuel's reading is probably right, that the angel stretched out his hand towards Jerusalem; the word God here stands in for Jehovah, which is itself a misreading of part of the Hebrew of Samuel. The added clause about the Lord beholding as the angel destroyed is absent from Samuel, and Ellicott cites Bertheau's judgment that it softens the harshness of the transition from the command to the countermand. He adds that it does not appear Jerusalem was touched at all, and that the halt, by the Hebrew accentuation, reads Enough now: drop thine hand.

The vision of the angel in the air is where the two books part company most sharply, and both the grammarians defend the fuller text. Delitzsch holds that the Chronicle tells this whole sequence at greater length than Samuel, which is circumstantial only about the negotiation for the threshingfloor, and that in substance the two accounts perfectly correspond, the Chronicle merely preserving subordinate details the other passes over. Ellicott makes the same case on stylistic grounds: the verse is not in Samuel, but nothing in its manner suggests a later hand, and it is as likely that the compiler of Samuel abridged the original as that the chronicler embellished it; Samuel does after all record the essential fact that David saw the angel that smote the people. The sword stretched out over the city uses a term employed elsewhere for the menace of divine wrath. The elders appear here without introduction, but a king would travel with a retinue of nobles, and their presence squares with Samuel's note that Araunah saw the king and his servants approaching. The sackcloth, Ellicott says, is the garb of mourners and penitents; Wesley has them humbling themselves for their sins and deprecating the wrath against the people.

David's plea is examined clause by clause. Ellicott finds the opening question about having commanded the numbering absent from Samuel, perhaps added for clearness, perhaps part of the original; the confession of having sinned and done evil may be paraphrastic beside Samuel's blunter I have dealt crookedly, but is hardly a corruption of it. The appeal for the sheep is verbatim in both, except that Samuel lacks the address O Lord my God — the flock is named without the article, and the king was the shepherd. The closing words asking that the people not be plagued run in a strange Hebrew order, which makes Ellicott suspect two marginal glosses that have crept into the text.
18:
The order to build comes through two intermediaries, and Henry makes that the point. The angel who had carried on the war is the first to set the treaty of peace on foot, for angels do not desire the woeful day; and though he could have spoken to David directly, he passed the word through the seer instead, putting an honour upon the prophetic office, as the revelation of Jesus Christ was notified by an angel to John and by John to the churches. Both Henry and Wesley then read the command itself as the pardon: being told to build an altar was a blessed token of reconciliation, since had God been pleased to kill the man he would never have appointed a sacrifice he did not mean to accept. Ellicott renders the clause as a pluperfect — the angel had told Gad to tell David — and notes that Samuel knows nothing of the angel's mediation, having simply Gad coming to David that day. He treats angelic mediation between God and the prophets as a mark of the later books of the Canon, while listing passages in Judges and Genesis that cut against the rule. The following verse he dismisses as a variation of one tittle, the small projection of a letter mentioned in Matt. 5:18.

Then comes the hinge of the chapter's textual troubles: what Ornan looked up and saw. Ellicott says there can be little doubt the Hebrew here is corrupt and that Samuel is right, where Araunah sees the king and his servants passing by; the words for returned and looked up, and those for angel and king, are near enough to be confused in an ill-written manuscript, and both the Greek and the Latin read king. Clarke assembles the same evidence at greater length, with the Syriac and Arabic making David the one who saw the angel, one of Kennicott's manuscripts reading king, and Houbigant defending that reading from the parallel in Samuel, where Ornan is said to see David and nothing is said of his seeing an angel. On Houbigant's reconstruction the two verses describe two moments, the king sighted at a distance and the king arriving in the floor, so that Ornan and his sons first hid in fear of the royal visit and then had to present themselves. Henry and Wesley read the text as it stands and keep the angel: Ornan had seen him, and the sight so terrified him and his four sons that they hid, unable to bear the brightness of that glory and afraid of the drawn sword, dreading what vengeance was coming on their family.

Ellicott notes that the clause about Ornan threshing wheat sits awkwardly beside what precedes it, yet is probably genuine, since a threshingfloor is where the man belongs, and the Greek adds to Samuel that the pestilence fell in the days of wheat harvest. The verse in which David arrives and is recognised is likewise missing from Samuel, and he judges that the corruption of the previous verse made some such statement necessary here.

The request itself is a plea rather than a command — pray give me the place of the threshingfloor — and where Samuel has Araunah ask why his lord the king has come, this account puts the stipulation of a full price into David's mouth from the start. Ellicott hears behind it the purchase of the cave of Machpelah, and thinks the recollection of that bargain may have shaped the present wording. Henry draws the plain moral: David would not serve God at other people's charge.
23:
Ornan's answer is generous past the request, and Ellicott reads it as the chronicler filling out a shorter original. Where Samuel has the owner say only take and offer, this text makes him say take and do, a difference of a single Hebrew letter in a verb that can carry either sense; the explicit I give thee is an exegetical addition; and the list of gifts grows, the drags for fuel named by a word found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible but in one line of Isaiah and the parallel in Samuel, and the wheat for the meal offering added here, which Ellicott nevertheless thinks probably belonged to the oldest form of the story. Samuel keeps a clause this account drops, the owner's parting blessing that the Lord his God accept the king. The refusal is likewise firmer here: not merely at a price but at a full price, with a reason Samuel lacks. Ellicott endorses it in Ewald's words, that it was of the essence of sacrifice to surrender something valued in order to win from God a greater good.

Then the sum, and the chapter's hardest numerical problem. Ellicott states the discrepancy without softening it: six hundred shekels of gold here, fifty shekels of silver in Samuel, two estimates obviously discordant, and no way to arbitrate between them, since neither the extent of the ground nor the value of the sums is known. He measures both against the price paid for the field and cave of Machpelah and finds fifty shekels of silver too little and six hundred of gold far too high for a threshingfloor, so that perhaps gold should be read as silver. He reports and then rejects the harmonising proposal that the two writers were pricing different things, Samuel the floor and the oxen and the chronicler the whole temple mount of Moriah; the texts themselves identify what was bought, since the place here is the place of the threshingfloor there. Since gold money is not otherwise attested among the Hebrews, on Madden's authority, he concludes that this is probably the later form of the tradition, while allowing that the chronicler doubtless preserved what he found in his source. He closes with a Babylonian contract tablet in which a house and grounds fetched the equivalent of six hundred and ninety shekels of silver in the last king of Babylon's second year. Wesley harmonises instead, reading the fifty shekels of gold in Samuel as gold to the value of six hundred shekels of silver. Delitzsch declines the question here and refers it to his own note on Samuel.

The fire that answers the prayer closes the account, and here the voices agree. Delitzsch observes that Samuel ends briefly, saying only that the Lord was entreated for the land, while this fuller telling unfolds what being entreated meant: David called, and the answer came as fire upon the altar of burnt offering, after which the sword went back into its sheath. He takes the sheathing as a figure for the stopping of the pestilence and the fire as the visible assurance that the prayer was heard and the offering graciously accepted, holding that earlier instances of the same sign put its reality beyond doubt. Ellicott points to the same precedents, Elijah's sacrifice among them, and calls this one the divine inauguration of a new altar and a new place of sacrifice as well as a sign that the prayer was heard. Clarke reads it as proof that God was now pacified towards the king and the people. Wesley presses it furthest: the fire that might justly have fastened on the sinner fastened on the sacrifice and consumed it, as Christ was made sin and a curse for us, and it pleased the Lord to bruise him, that through him God might be to us not a consuming fire but a reconciled Father.
27:
The sword going back into its sheath is the last act of the judgment, and Ellicott refuses to let it be read as mere imagery. It seems to him hardly fair to call the verse a figurative or poetical expression for the cessation of the plague, since David had just seen the angel with the sword drawn, and the older account equally treats him as a real concrete being and not a personification, whatever Reuss will have. The word for sheath occurs nowhere else, though a very similar Aramaic term is used in Daniel for the body as the sheath of the soul, and Ellicott thinks that form should perhaps be read here. Gill puts the same two acts together from the other end: God had accepted the prayer, as the Targum says, and answered it by bringing fire down on the sacrifice to consume it and by ordering the angel to put up his sword.

What follows, Ellicott notes, has no counterpart in Samuel, though the writer no doubt found some basis for it in his own special source; its business is to explain how a threshingfloor came to be a permanent sanctuary and the site ordained for the future Temple, and so to form a transition to the preparations for the building. The continuity is the point of the remark that David sacrificed there: the use of the floor as a place of sacrifice was kept up from the time the pestilence ceased, the answer by fire having been an unmistakable intimation of the divine will that it should be so. Wesley puts it as a simple inference the king drew — perceiving that this sacrifice was acceptable, he went on offering more in that place. Gill pauses over the owner's name, the same as the form in Samuel with a small variation of letters, both signifying, as Hillerus observes, the ornus, the pine tree or the ash.

The explanation offered for all this is an absence: the tabernacle Moses made, and the altar of burnt offering with it, were standing at that season in the high place at Gibeon. Gill is careful about the making, which was by the command of God and according to his direction. Ellicott sets the two sanctuaries against each other, the old dwelling-place of Jehovah over against the new one in Ornan's floor, and glosses the enquiring David could not perform as seeking God's favour by sacrifice and prayer. Gill adds the awkward admission that Gibeon was nonetheless the proper place to seek the Lord in.

Why the king could not go there is the chapter's last dispute, and four answers stand side by side. Ellicott quotes Keil for the first, that David could not go because of the sword of the angel, meaning the pestilence raging at Gibeon; he reports a second, that the awful vision had struck the king with some bodily weakness; and he prefers a third, that the menacing aspect of the apparition simply overawed him, so that he durst not follow the usual course, the sight leaving an indelible impression on his mind as to the sanctity of the place where it appeared. Clarke makes the fear practical: whether terror of the destroying angel or dread of the delay the journey would cost, David would not risk the people being exterminated while he travelled, and so built an altar hastily where he stood, and the fire from heaven showed his act and his devotion accepted. Wesley's version is the same calculation stated as a watch kept: with the angel standing over Jerusalem with drawn sword, he durst not leave the city, and thought it proper to worship in the place God had consecrated by his special presence and acceptance. Clarke draws the wider conclusion that such interventions must necessarily maintain in the people a full persuasion of the truth and divine origin of their religion.
